ahimsa: Ahimsa is the principle of nonviolence or non-harming, central to the Indian traditions of Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. More than simply refraining from physical violence, it is often understood as a discipline of thought and speech that avoids cruelty in every form. Mahatma Gandhi made ahimsa the basis of his political practice, holding that nonviolent resistance could transform both the resister and the opponent.
atman-brahman: In the Hindu Upanishads, atman is the innermost self or true essence of a person, and Brahman is the ultimate reality underlying the universe. A central teaching of Advaita Vedanta holds that atman and Brahman are ultimately one: to know your deepest self is to realize identity with ultimate reality. Liberation (moksha) is said to come from this realization, which dissolves ignorance about what we really are.
atomism: Atomism is the ancient theory, associated with Democritus and later Epicurus, that reality consists of tiny indivisible particles moving in empty space, with everything else, including minds and souls, arising from their combinations. Nothing exists except atoms and the void, so even death and chance can be explained without appealing to gods or cosmic purposes. Epicurus added random swerves of the atoms to make room for free action.
authenticity: Authenticity is the ideal of being true to yourself: living from your own values and choices rather than merely conforming to what society expects. Existentialists like Sartre and Heidegger made it central, arguing that since no ready-made script exists for a human life, authenticity requires honest self-awareness and owning your choices. Critics such as Charles Taylor add that self-creation still needs horizons of significance beyond the self.
bad-faith: Bad faith is Sartre's term for self-deception: pretending to oneself that one is not free. A person in bad faith hides behind a role, blames circumstance or temperament, or acts as if their choices were fixed facts about the world. Sartre held we are condemned to be free, so fleeing that freedom is a constant temptation, exemplified by his famous waiter who behaves as a mere machine.
buddhism: Buddhism is a tradition founded in ancient India by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, or awakened one. It teaches that life involves dissatisfaction or suffering, that this arises from craving and attachment, and that freedom comes through ethical conduct, meditation, and wisdom. Central doctrines include impermanence, non-self, karma, and rebirth, and many schools exist, from Theravada to Zen and Tibetan Buddhism.
buddhist-compassion: Compassion (karuna) is, in Buddhism, the heartfelt wish that others be free from suffering, and a core virtue to be cultivated alongside loving-kindness. Because Buddhist teaching denies sharp separations between selves, many hold that compassion is not optional benevolence but the natural response to seeing all beings as interconnected. In Mahayana Buddhism, the bodhisattva vows to work for the liberation of all beings before resting in final liberation.
buddhist-impermanence: Impermanence (anicca) is the Buddhist teaching that everything conditioned, from bodies and feelings to relationships and civilizations, is constantly changing and passes away. Nothing lasting can be relied upon, and on the Buddhist diagnosis our suffering arises largely from clinging to things that cannot stay. Recognizing impermanence is therefore not pessimism but part of wisdom: it loosens attachment rather than, as many stress, sliding into nihilism.
buddhist-karma: Karma is the Indian idea, adopted and reworked by Buddhism, that intentional actions have consequences that shape one's future, in this life or, within the rebirth framework, in lives to come. Wholesome actions rooted in generosity lead toward well-being; harmful actions rooted in greed and hatred deepen suffering. Karma is not fate or divine punishment: on the Buddhist view it is a natural causal process that can be changed.
buddhist-non-self: Non-self (anatman) is the Buddhist doctrine that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul behind our experiences. What we call I is, on this view, a shifting bundle of processes, including body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness, with no fixed essence. Many hold this does not deny that persons exist, but denies they are the solid, enduring things we take them to be.
faith-vs-reason: The relation between faith and reason asks whether religious belief can be rationally justified, and how it stands toward evidence and argument. Some traditions hold that faith and reason harmonize, as Aquinas did; others, like Kierkegaard and William James, argue faith reaches where reason cannot; skeptics such as Clifford hold that belief without sufficient evidence is never warranted. Many note that even science rests on assumptions reason cannot finally prove.
four-noble-truths: The Four Noble Truths are the Buddha's foundational diagnosis and prescription: first, that life involves suffering or unsatisfactoriness (dukkha); second, that suffering arises from craving and attachment; third, that suffering can cease; and fourth, that the path to its cessation is the Noble Eightfold Path of ethical conduct, meditation, and wisdom. Often compared to a physician's diagnosis, they frame the whole Buddhist project of liberation.
immortality: Immortality is the continued existence of a person after bodily death, traditionally grounded in an immortal soul, a view defended from Plato through Descartes and in many religious traditions. Philosophers debate what would make the surviving being you (memory? consciousness?), whether an eternal life would eventually become tedious, and whether death really harms the one who dies, as Epicurus famously argued it does not.
kant-autonomy: For Kant, autonomy of the will is the capacity to be a self-legislating moral agent: to act on principles you rationally endorse yourself, rather than on external authority, impulse, or mere obedience. A morally worthy action is thus one freely willed according to a universal moral law, not done from compulsion or fear. Autonomy, on this view, is the very ground of human dignity.
meaning-of-life: The question of life's meaning asks whether human life has purpose, significance, or value, and if so where these come from. Religious answers locate meaning in God or a cosmic order; existentialists like Sartre and Camus hold there is no given meaning, so we must create our own; philosophers such as Susan Wolf propose that meaning comes from loving engagement with things genuinely worth engaging.
nihilism: Nihilism is the view that life, values, and meaning lack any objective grounding: there are no genuine purposes, no binding moral facts. Nietzsche, its most famous analyst, saw nihilism as the crisis following the death of God, the collapse of the frameworks that once gave life meaning. Responses range from despair to Nietzsche's call to create new values and Camus's defiant embrace of the absurd.
philosopher-king: The philosopher king is Plato's proposal in the Republic that the ideal city be ruled by philosophers, those who possess knowledge of the Good, rather than by the ambitious or the wealthy. Only such rulers, Plato believed, free from private interest and guided by wisdom, could govern justly. The idea has drawn lasting criticism: power can corrupt anyone, and concentrated authority without checks is dangerous.
religious-pluralism: Religious pluralism is the view that more than one religion can offer a genuine path to ultimate reality, so no single tradition holds an exclusive claim on truth. It contrasts with exclusivism, which says only one religion is true, and inclusivism, which says one is fullest though others are partially valid. Philosophers like John Hick defend pluralism, while critics argue it flattens real doctrinal differences and may be self-undermining.
second-order-desires: Second-order desires are desires about your own desires: wanting to want something, or being glad or ashamed of what you want. Philosopher Harry Frankfurt argued that what makes us persons, rather than mere wantons driven by whatever we feel, is the capacity to evaluate our first-order desires and identify our will with some of them. This idea has shaped debates on free will, personhood, and moral responsibility.
stoicism: Stoicism is an ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, associated with Zeno, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius, teaching that virtue is the only true good and that tranquility comes from focusing on what is within our control. External things such as wealth, reputation, and even health are indifferents; what matters is how we respond. On the Stoic view, disturbing emotions arise from mistaken judgments, so reshaping our judgments reshapes our emotions.
the-absurd: The absurd, in Camus's sense, is the clash between the human longing for meaning, clarity, and permanence and a universe that offers none. Camus argued we should neither flee into false hope nor despair, but live in lucid revolt; his image is Sisyphus, happy as he endlessly rolls his boulder. The absurd thus names both a predicament and a possible stance toward it, rather than a settled doctrine.
transcendental-idealism: Transcendental idealism is Kant's view that we know the world only as it appears to us, structured by the mind's own forms of space, time, and concepts, never as things are in themselves. He compared it to a Copernican revolution: objects must conform to our knowledge rather than the reverse. Kant did not deny that reality exists; he denied that we can know it apart from the mind's structuring.
utopia-dystopia: Utopia is the imagination of an ideally ordered society; dystopia is its dark mirror, a society that promised perfection but delivered oppression. The genre, from Plato's Republic through More's Utopia to Orwell and Atwood, works as social criticism: by projecting ideals or fears onto imagined worlds, it exposes dangers latent in real ones. Many dystopias warn precisely that enforced utopias become nightmares.
zen: Zen is a school of Mahayana Buddhism, developed in China and Japan, that emphasizes direct experience and meditation (zazen) over scriptural study and abstract theory. It teaches that awakening, seeing things as they are, can arrive suddenly, and it often uses paradox, koans, and everyday activities to break habitual, conceptual thinking. Central ideals include no-mind (mushin), spontaneity, and the dissolution of the self-other divide.
